title: School staff wrestled with 'anxiety and dread' before emaciated teen's rescue
summary: Court records show an Ottawa school asked police to do a wellness check on a student who was found to be severely malnourished. The school had previously reached out to the Children's Aid Society of…

image.caption: The Ottawa Courthouse on Elgin Street in September 2022. Earlier this week, an Ottawa mother was sentenced to nine years in prison after pleading guilty to criminal negligence causing bodily harm. Police found her emaciated 18-year-old son forcibly confined to a bed earlier this year. (Matthew Kupfe

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains graphic details about child abuse and animal abuse.

Staff at an Ottawa school who called on police to do the wellness check that led to the rescue of a severely malnourished 18-year-old earlier this year did so after months of "suffocating anxiety and dread" about the growing absence of the complex-needs student.

They also contacted police because when they had previously reached out to the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa (CASO), when the teen was a minor, the school was "dissatisfied" with CASO's response, a courtroom heard this week.
"I knew something wasn't right," one school employee said in court about the days, weeks and months that passed without the teen coming to school.
Another recalled that after a distressing update from the teen's mother, she lay awake at night "haunted by thoughts of what he was enduring."
"Something in our system needs to change so that there are checks and balances so that [vulnerable students] cannot just disappear," she added.
CASO said it doesn't comment on specific cases or actions taken, citing confidentiality.

"However, we can assure you that every report concerning the safety and well-being of a child is carefully assessed through a child protection and safety lens," the organization said in an email to CBC News on Friday.

"The Society's priority is always the evaluation of potential risk to a child, and all concerns are reviewed and responded to in accordance with applicable child protection standards, legislation and professional practices."
'Difficult to imagine a more vulnerable human'

On Tuesday, the teen's mother pleaded guilty to criminal negligence causing bodily harm, failing to provide the necessaries of life, and failing to care for a family cat that was found dead by the teen's bedside.
The judge sentenced her to nine years in prison for the first conviction and shorter concurrent sentences for the other two.

According to an agreed statement of facts read out in court, police discovered the teen, who is now 19, in January 2026. He was found in what court heard described as a boarded-up "cage bed" in a decrepit basement bedroom.

Though he was 18 and therefore an adult at the time of his rescue, "it's difficult to imagine a more vulnerable human being," assistant Crown attorney Louise Tansey said. The teen was born with a rare genetic disorder affecting his speech, movement and cognitive development. He is also prone to seizures.
"He will forever remain childlike, forever in that vulnerable state," Tansey said.

items: Teen was 'near death' when his school asked police for a wellness check, court hears

blocks.text: In the fall of 2025, the teen remained absent from school amid a series of red flags about his family situation. But as detailed in the victim impact statements read out by three school staff members on Tuesday, the concerns about his well-being stretched over years.

And even after the vice-principal shared the good news about the teen being removed from the home, the relief school staff felt was coupled with shock over the teen's condition — and guilt over not having sounded the alarm sooner.
"How I wish I never sent him home the last day of school the previous June, " the first staff member said.
Out of sight
Neither the teen nor his mother can be identified under a publication ban.
The first staff member said she worked with the teen one-on-one for years. He needed help to walk around but loved crawling on the floor during gym time.
"[He] isn’t a complicated guy. He has needs and wants like every other human, but if he’s fed, clean, well-dressed and loved, he is beyond happy," she said.
According to the second staff member, "the decline in the care that [he] was receiving from home," plus the amount of time he was being kept at home, compelled staff to push for a wellness check.

It was an agonizing dilemma that tortured all of us who cared for him, always suspecting the worst but not having any factual evidence. We needed to tread lightly for fear that we would not ever see him again.School staff member

The growing boy who'd been "a smiley, chubby-cheeked [and] active" student began showing up to school with bruises and a "ravenous" appetite, "desperately eating as if every meal might be his last," the third staff member said.
Staff were once told he'd fallen down the stairs at home after his chair locks were disengaged, but there was no damage to the chair, she said.
"A suffocating anxiety and dread took hold of every staff member watching this sweet boy wither away before our eyes," she said.
The school spoke to the mother often, provided the family gift cards and, when the funding for that ran out, staff bought food and other supplies with their own money.

"We would drop them off at his home hoping to catch a glimpse of our smiley friend," the third staff member continued. "Unfortunately, each time we would go to drop off things at home, we were not allowed to see [him]. [She] would always meet us outside the house."
Children's Aid Society contacted
According to the agreed statement of facts, the school contacted the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa in 2024 because the teen had appeared gaunt and pale.

He missed a lot of school that fall, and when a staff member ran into the mother at a store and went to see the teen who was waiting in the family's car, she was horrified by his "shockingly emaciated" appearance, the third staff member said.
It's unclear how CASO responded when contacted in 2024. The school reached out to CASO again at a later point when the teen was now 18, the third staff member said.
"[CASO] stated they could not act because he was [an adult] and suggested a police wellness check," she said.

blocks.text: According to the agreed statement of facts, "the school was dissatisfied with [CASO's] response to their concerns and so on Jan. 21, 2026, they contacted the Ottawa Police for assistance."

In a statement emailed to CBC News on Thursday, the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa said it can't comment on, confirm or deny any involvement with specific people or families, adding that child welfare records are confidential.
The organization confirmed that once a young person reaches their 18th birthday, they are no longer subject to the child protection provisions of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act.
Not much was shared in court Tuesday about the mother's background.
Oliver Abergel, the lawyer representing her that day, said she was abandoned by her mother and grew up with a father who was not particularly present.

"I can only imagine that the background did not help, and it's not being offered as an excuse," Abergel said, adding that the mother "was not particularly interested in having a violin brought out for her" and has accepted responsibility for her crimes.
Abergel did not say whether the mother struggled as a result of any systemic gaps to getting her son the care he needed.
But in a letter of support filed with the court and which was provided to CBC News on Friday afternoon, the mother's aunt wrote that the mother needed help and still needs help, "not jail time."
The death of the mother's own grandmother hit her hard, according to the aunt.
"Our entire family kept saying ... [she] would not be able to handle it but she kept saying she would never abandon her children like her mother did and honestly she did her best."

"I know she could have reached out to an organization for help but honestly I think she just wanted to prove everyone wrong who doubted her and unfortunately went about it the wrong way," the aunt added. "What she did wasn't malicious. It was a cry for help. I'm not saying it was right but it definitely wasn't intentional."
The mother's guilty pleas spared the court a potentially lengthy trial and witnesses being re-traumatized, the lawyer who represented her Tuesday said. (Guy Quenneville/CBC)

In response to a request to talk about what supports are available for caregivers of complex-needs teens who turn adult, CASO wrote that that transition "can create challenges in situations where vulnerable young adults continue to require significant care, supervision or support but no longer fall within the child welfare system's protection mandate."

"In such circumstances, concerns about an adult's safety or wellbeing may fall under the responsibility of other community systems, including health care providers, developmental services, community agencies, adult protective supports where available or police services when there are immediate safety concerns," CASO added in its written statement.

There is ongoing discussion across Ontario and Canada about the need for strong transition planning and "enhanced services" for youth with complex needs as they age out of the children's systems, the organization added.
Stopped coming to school
For staff at the teen's school, the decision to contact CASO was not easy, according to the third staff member.

"[Some] staff were so worried that we would strain the relationship with the mom and that she would pull him from school," she said, adding that the school later learned the mother was "furious" CASO had checked in on the family.
"[She] had told his support workers that once [her son] turned 18, she wasn’t required to send him back [to school]. This threw my colleagues and I into a panic," she added.
By the fall of 2025, the teen had stopped showing up to school altogether and CHEO had lost contact with the mother, court heard.

The school called and emailed the mother weekly. "In one response, she claimed [her son] refused to come upstairs to eat and that she refused to bring food down to his basement room," the third staff member said.

In October 2025, one of the teen's teachers offered to send a personal support worker to the family's home to help get him ready for school. "There was no response," according to the agreed statement of facts.
Two months later, when hospital staff went to deliver a new stroller, the mother would not let them inside their home. She also refused the school's delivery of a new wheelchair in January 2026.

In arguing for the nine-year sentence on the criminal negligence charge — which was a joint submission with the defence — Tansey, the Crown attorney, described the mother's behaviour as "deprivation being paired with preventing others from rendering life-saving assistance."
'An indelible scar on my soul'
The night before school resumed in January 2026, the teen's mother told staff that he would not be returning to class and that she was placing him in a home.
"Our fears had come true," the third staff member said.
She was no longer on staff at the school, but she and others encouraged the school's vice-principal to call police and ask for a wellness check, she said.

"I wrestled with making that call, terrified of losing the relationship that kept a link to him," she said. "It was an agonizing dilemma that tortured all of us who cared for him, always suspecting the worst but not having any factual evidence. We needed to tread lightly for fear that we would not ever see him again."
The horror of knowing he endured extended starvation, solitary confinement, and severe cruelty in that basement leaves an indelible scar on my soul.School staff member

Police went to the home on Jan. 21 and found the teen in dire condition. The agreed statement of facts lists a host of medical issues, including severe respiratory failure, infestation by bugs and renal failure.
"Police, when they attended, thought they had discovered a body," Tansey said.
The teen is now back at school but can't crawl on the gym floor anymore because his legs suffered substantial atrophy and contractures from his time in confinement, the second staff member said.
When she visited him in the hospital, "I apologized to him for taking so long," she told the courtroom, her voice racked with emotion.
The third staff member said the entire school community is grateful he survived.
But she added, "The horror of knowing he endured extended starvation, solitary confinement and severe cruelty in that basement leaves an indelible scar on my soul."

If you’re affected by this report, you can look for mental health support through resources in your province or territory . If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911.
